extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Kant's Groundwork
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Kant's criteria about the moral law, the status of freedom, the object of practical reason, and the distinction between good/evil and welfare as presented in the Groundwork. Focused on conceptual/practical standards Kant uses to justify moral claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law is a priori and apodeictically certain
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law is given as a fact of pure reason of which we are a priori conscious, and which is apodeictically certain, though no example of its exact fulfilment is found in experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant insists the objective reality of the moral law cannot be proved by theoretical reason or a posteriori experience; its certainty is immediate in practical (moral) consciousness and does not require empirical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law cannot be established by theoretical deduction or experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective reality of the moral law cannot be proved by any deduction by theoretical reason, whether speculative or empirically supported, nor a posteriori by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to deduce morality from theoretical or empirical grounds are vain; the moral law must be accepted on practical a priori grounds rather than inferred from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law as basis for deducing freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of deriving the moral principle from theory, the moral principle serves conversely as the principle of the deduction of a faculty (freedom) which no experience could prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant treats the moral law as providing a practical demonstration of the possibility (and practical reality) of freedom — the moral law legitimates postulating freedom even when speculative reason cannot prove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law provides objective practical reality to noumenal causality
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law is a law of the causality of free agents and therefore of the possibility of a supersensible (intelligible) system of nature; it gives a positive definition to a causality that speculative reason previously conceived only negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical, not theoretical, enlargement of the concept of causality — the moral law turns a previously merely 'negative' notion of noumenal causality into something with objective practical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical use of reason converts transcendent ideas into immanent practical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law changes the transcendent use of reason into an immanent use, so that reason, by means of ideas, can be an efficient cause in the field of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant claims that while speculative reason's transcendent ambitions fail, practical reason supplies a legitimate immanent application of reason's ideas (e.g., freedom) to guide action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between phenomenal determinism and noumenal freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Although experience shows no example of absolute spontaneity, we can consistently regard actions as subject to physical conditions as phenomena while regarding the agent's causality as physically unconditioned as a noumenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits a practical postulation of freedom compatible with observed deterministic laws of nature: on the phenomenal level behaviour is causally determined, while noumenally the will can be free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reason fills speculative gaps without enlarging theoretical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reason does not give speculative reason theoretical insight into supersensible things, but it supplies certainty about the problematical notion of freedom by giving it objective (practical) reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral law legitimates certain postulates (e.g., freedom) for moral purposes without claiming to provide theoretical knowledge of noumena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories (e.g., causality) have practical but not theoretical application to supersensible objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective reality of a pure concept of the understanding in the supersensible gives practical reality to the other categories only insofar as they relate to the determining principle of the will; they do not expand theoretical knowledge of such beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may legitimately apply categories to intelligences in a practical manner (for moral purposes), but this does not authorize speculative metaphysical claims about the nature of supersensible objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of practical reason defined as an effect producible through freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: A concept of the practical reason is the idea of an object as an effect possible to be produced through freedom; deciding whether something is an object of pure practical reason is discerning the possibility of willing the action that would realize it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If we take the object as determining our desire, we must consider physical possibility; if the law (a priori) determines action, judgement depends on moral possibility (would we will it if we had the power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between moral possibility and physical possibility in evaluating objects
rubrics_metrics.description: If the object is taken as determining desire, one must know whether it is physically possible by the free use of our powers before judging it an object of practical reason; if the law is a priori the judgement does not depend on physical power but on whether we would will the action if we had the power (moral possibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether something counts as an object of pure practical reason, distinguish: (a) empirical/physical feasibility when desire drives action, (b) moral permissibility/possibility when an a priori law governs the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only 'good' and 'evil' are objects of practical reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The only objects of practical reason are therefore those of good and evil: the former necessarily desired according to a principle of reason, the latter necessarily shunned according to a principle of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reason's domain is normative (good/evil); non-normative objects (mere welfare, pleasure) belong to sensibility and do not serve as ultimate objects of pure practical reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good in itself must be independent of sensation (not mere pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the notion of good is to serve as foundation of practical law, it cannot be derived from pleasure (sensation), because we cannot discern a priori what ideas will be accompanied with pleasure; thus what is primarily good cannot be grounded in sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat goods that are merely means to pleasure as 'welfare' (das Wohl) rather than 'good' (das Gute). A genuine 'good' must be assessable by reason and not contingent upon individual sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate moral 'good/evil' from welfare 'weal/woe'
rubrics_metrics.description: Good or evil always implies a reference to the will as determined by law of reason, whereas well or ill (weal/woe) imply reference to our condition (pleasure or pain); moral judgement requires reason not mere sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'good/evil' for judgments about the will and its maxims; use 'weal/woe' for judgments about consequences to our sensibility. Moral evaluation aims at universal, communicable principles, not subjective pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral value attaches to maxims and persons, not to things or sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Good and evil properly refer to actions, the maxim of the will, and consequently the acting person himself as a good or evil man, and not to a thing or to sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral worth by examining maxims and the will's conformity to law (not by the pleasantness or unpleasantness of outcomes). A painful experience can be morally neutral or even good if it stems from a right maxim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pure practical law (a priori) from rational practical precepts tied to inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: Either a rational principle is conceived as the determining principle of the will (a practical a priori law), in which case the action is good in itself; or the maxim is consequent on a principle of desire (object of pleasure), in which case the action is only relatively good and not a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only maxims determined by pure practical law (a priori, legislative form) confer absolute moral worth; actions motivated by inclination or utility are only relatively good as means to other ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rule: determine 'good' after establishing the moral law
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of good and evil must not be determined before the moral law but only after it and by means of it; to assume the concept of good as foundation would illegitimately presuppose what is to be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical method requires first asking whether the will has a priori determining principles; defining 'good' empirically would preclude establishing a priori moral laws. Do not circularly ground law on a pre-assumed concept of good.
